q:
A 32-year-old woman presents with acute pain and redness of the left eye associated with marked photophobia and blurred vision. Slit-lamp examination reveals ciliary injection, inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber, keratic precipitates, and a small sluggishly reacting pupil. She is diagnosed with anterior uveitis and started on appropriate anti-inflammatory treatment. Which of the following drugs should
be added to reduce ciliary spasm and prevent posterior synechiae formation?
e: A long-acting antimuscarinic producing mydriasis and cycloplegia. In anterior uveitis, antimuscarinic agents are used to prevent posterior synechiae between the iris and lens and to relieve painful ciliary muscle spasm.

q:
A 67-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of
severe pain and redness in her right eye associated with marked diminution of vision, headache, nausea, and repeated vomiting. Examination reveals a shallow anterior
chamber and markedly elevated intraocular pressure, suggesting an acute
angle-closure  glaucoma. The ophthalmologist wants to achieve a rapid short-term reduction in the markedly elevated intraocular pressure before definitive treatment. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate?
e:
Mannitol is an osmotic agent used for short-term management of acute rises in
intraocular pressure.

q:
A 56-year-old man with a history of severe bronchial asthma undergoes abdominal
surgery under general anesthesia. Several hours after surgery, he develops suprapubic discomfort, lower abdominal fullness, and inability to pass urine despite a strong urge to void. Examination reveals a palpable distended urinary bladder. There is no evidence of mechanical urinary tract obstruction. Which of the following drugs can be used in this condition?
e: Tamsulosin is a selective α₁-blocker that reduces urethral/bladder-outlet smooth-muscle tone. Selective α-blockade can be used along with bladder decompression in postoperative urinary retention to facilitate subsequent voiding.

q:
A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after accidentally
ingesting an agricultural insecticide that had been stored in an unlabelled bottle. Within an hour, she develops profuse sweating, excessive salivation, lacrimation, repeated vomiting, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea. On examination, her pupils
are markedly constricted, pulse rate is 46/min, and she has diffuse wheezing with copious bronchial secretions. Which of the following statements is not correct
regarding this clinical scenario?
o: Carbamates are reversible inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase.
Atropine can be used in both organophosphate and carbamate poisoning
Pralidoxime has a very good therapeutic effect in carbamate poisoning.
Atropine cannot treat the skeletal muscle weakness seen in this patient.

q: A 72-year-old man is brought by his daughter because of gradually progressive memory impairment over the past 2 years. He repeatedly asks the same questions, frequently misplaces household objects, and has recently begun forgetting familiar appointments and routes. His symptoms have progressed slowly, without focal neurological deficits or fluctuations in consciousness. Cognitive assessment confirms impairment predominantly involving recent episodic memory, and further evaluation supports early Alzheimer disease. The neurologist considers a disease-modifying monoclonal antibody therapy directed against amyloid-β plaques. Which of the following drugs has this mechanism?
e: Aducanumab is a human monoclonal antibody targeting amyloid-β that reduces amyloid plaque burden.

q: A 29-year-old woman presents with progressive drooping of both eyelids and intermittent double vision for the past several months. Her symptoms are minimal in the morning but become markedly worse by evening. She also reports difficulty chewing toward the end of meals, occasional nasal speech, and weakness while combing her hair. Examination shows bilateral ptosis that worsens after sustained upward gaze, fatigable proximal muscle weakness, normal pupils, intact sensation, and preserved deep-tendon reflexes. Her muscle strength improves after a period of rest. For long-term symptomatic management of this condition, which of the following drugs is most appropriate?
e: Pyridostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase, thereby preserving acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction and improving neuromuscular transmission. It is a standard symptomatic treatment for myasthenia gravis

q: After passing the extra attempt of the FMG examination held on October 31, a group of students plans a trip to Leh, Ladakh. They hire a car from Delhi and begin their journey. Soon after the car starts moving, one of the students develops progressive nausea, a sensation of dizziness, and repeated episodes of vomiting, particularly while the vehicle is moving along winding roads. Which of the following drugs can be used in this patient?

A 74-year-old woman with dementia is brought by her daughter because she has
developed a sudden compelling urge to pass urine that is difficult to defer, associated with increased daytime frequency, nocturia, and occasional leakage of urine before reaching the toilet. She has no dysuria or fever, and urinalysis shows no evidence of infection. She is diagnosed with overactive bladder. Which of the following
antimuscarinic drugs can be used in this patient?
e: Trospium is a quaternary antimuscarinic agent used for overactive bladder. Goodman & Gilman specifically notes that CNS-related antimuscarinic effects are less likely with trospium, making it the best option among these antimuscarinics when cognitive adverse effects are an important concern

q: A 43-year-old woman presents with recurrent painful involuntary contractions of the neck muscles, causing persistent rotation of her head to one side and difficulty maintaining a neutral head position. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. She is treated with local Botox injections into the affected neck muscles, with marked improvement in the abnormal movements. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the drug used in this patient?
o: Blocks transport of acetylcholine into synaptic vesicles
Blocks release of acetylcholine from presynaptic nerve terminals
Inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
e: Botox is a botulinum toxin preparation. It enters cholinergic nerve terminals and cleaves SNARE proteins, thereby preventing vesicular acetylcholine release and producing temporary local muscle paralysis. It is used in conditions such as cervical dystonia

q: A 36-year-old woman receives an intravenous antibiotic in the emergency department. Within minutes, she develops generalized urticaria, intense pruritus, swelling of the lips and tongue, hoarseness, diffuse wheezing, and severe breathlessness. She becomes dizzy and confused. Her pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 72/44 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment in this patient?
e: Intramuscular epinephrine 1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh is the first-line treat- ment for anaphylaxis. In adults, the usual dose is 0.5 mg IM.

q: A 24-year-old man with persistent bronchial asthma is using a combination inhaler containing budesonide and formoterol. His asthma control improves significantly. During follow-up, the physician explains the potential adverse effects produced by the bronchodilator component of his inhaler. Which of the following is the least likely side effect caused by the bronchodilator used in this patient?
e: β₂-agonists cause hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia, by promoting movement of potassium into skeletal muscle cells. Therefore, hyperkalemia is the least likely adverse effect.

q: A 76-year-old woman with moderate dementia is brought by her daughter because of progressively troublesome urinary symptoms. She passes urine very frequently during the day, wakes several times at night to void, and experiences a sudden compelling urge to urinate that is difficult to postpone. On several occasions, she has leaked urine before reaching the toilet. Urinalysis is normal, and there is no evidence of urinary tract infection or mechanical obstruction. Because of her pre-existing cognitive impairment, the physician starts mirabegron for symptomatic relief. This drug mainly causes relief in overactive bladder because it is acting through which of the following receptor/signalling mechanisms?
e: Mirabegron is a selective β3-adrenergic receptor agonist. β3 receptors couple principally to the Gs–adenylyl cyclase–cAMP pathway. Activation of β3 receptors in the urinary bladder relaxes the detrusor muscle and increases bladder capacity, relieving symptoms of overactive bladder.

q:
A 47-year-old woman reports recurrent episodes of severe pounding headache,
palpitations, profuse sweating, and tremulousness. During one such episode, her
blood pressure is 218/126 mmHg. Laboratory testing shows markedly elevated
catecholamine metabolites, and abdominal imaging reveals a well-defined tumor
arising from the adrenal medulla. Surgical removal of the tumor is planned. The
physician wants to control her episodic hypertension for 1–3 weeks before surgery. Which of the following drugs can be used for decreasing preoperative hypertension?
e: Phenoxybenzamine is an irreversible nonselective α-adrenergic antagonist commonly started 1–3 weeks before surgery to control severe hypertension and other effects of excess catechol- amines.

q: A 69-year-old man presents with a 1-year history of difficulty initiating urination, straining during micturition, a weak urinary stream, intermittency, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. He also reports increased urinary frequency and waking 3–4 times every night to pass urine. Digital rectal examination reveals a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate without nodules or tenderness. His blood pressure has consistently remained on the lower side, around 96/62 mmHg, and he occasionally experiences light-headedness on standing. The physician wants to provide rapid symptomatic relief by reducing the dynamic component of urinary outflow obstruction. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate for decreasing the dynamic component of the disease in this patient?
e: Tamsulosin preferentially targets the α₁A receptor subtype, which predominates in the pros- tate. It relaxes smooth muscle in the prostate, bladder neck, and prostatic urethra, rapidly re- ducing the dynamic component of obstruction. At recommended doses, it is less likely to cause orthostatic hypotension than many other α₁ blockers.

q: A 58-year-old man presents with a gradual, painless reduction in peripheral vision over the past several months. He denies acute eye pain, redness, or episodes of vomiting. Ophthalmic examination shows elevated intraocular pressure, increased optic-disc cupping, and peripheral visual-field loss. Gonioscopy demonstrates an open anterior chamber angle. He also has a history of  bronchial asthma with recurrent wheezing. The ophthalmologist wants to use a topical β-blocker to reduce intraocular pressure. Which of the following β-blockers can be used in this patient?
e: Betaxolol is a relatively β₁-selective adrenergic antagonist used in glaucoma. Compared with timolol, it has a lower incidence of respiratory adverse effects because it causes less pulmonary β₂ blockade.

q:
A 64-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, easy fatigability, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and bilateral pedal edema. On examination, he has an elevated JVP, bilateral basal crepitations, and an S3 gallop. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. As part of his treatment for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), spironolactone is added to his medications. After several months, he develops bilateral tender enlargement of the breasts and decreased libido. Which of the following mechanisms most likely
explains this adverse effect?
o: Activation of nuclear estrogen receptors ERα and ERβ with altered gene transcription
Inhibition of CYP17 and CYP11A, resulting in decreased steroidogenesis
Competitive antagonism of mineralocorticoid receptors in the distal nephron
e: Spironolactone has antiandrogenic activity. Goodman & Gilman describes it as a weak inhibitor of the androgen receptor and of testosterone synthesis. Its interaction with androgen and progesterone receptors contributes to gynecomastia, impotence, and menstrual abnormalities.

q:
A 27-year-old man travels from Delhi to Leh, Ladakh, with a rapid ascent to high altitude. Within several hours of arrival, he develops a severe headache, nausea, repeated vomiting, breathlessness, marked fatigue and difficulty concentrating.
Over the next few hours, his symptoms worsen and his friends notice that his judgment has become impaired. Which of the following is the best treatment in this patient?

A 63-year-old man with a history of ischemic heart disease is brought to the emergency department with sudden severe breathlessness that worsens on lying flat. He is
extremely anxious and tachypneic. On examination, respiratory rate is 34/min, oxygen saturation is 82% on room air, and bilateral diffuse fine crepitations are heard over the lung fields. He is coughing up pink, frothy sputum. Cardiac examination suggests acute left ventricular failure. Which of the following drugs can be used in this patient?
e: Acute left-sided heart failure with massive pulmonary congestion requires rapid therapy with an intravenous loop diuretic. Furosemide also acutely increases venous capacitance, thereby reducing left ventricular filling pressure even before significant diuresis occurs.

q: A 34-year-old man presents with marked polyuria and polydipsia, passing nearly 7–8 L of very dilute urine per day. His plasma osmolality is high-normal, while urine osmolality remains very low. After administration of desmopressin, there is little to no increase in urine osmolality. What is the mechanism of action of the drug that can be used in this condition?
o: It acts predominantly on the proximal convoluted tubule, causing increased sodium and water loss.
It acts on the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, causing increased sodium and water loss.
It acts on the distal convoluted tubule, causing mild sodium and water loss, which produces volume contraction and thereby increases proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption.
It blocks the ENaC channel in the cortical collecting duct, thereby decreasing sodium reabsorption.
e: Thiazides inhibit Na⁺-Cl⁻ transport in the DCT. The resulting mild volume contraction increases proximal tubular water reabsorption, reducing distal delivery and paradoxically decreasing urine volume.

q:
Which of the following does not act through the lumen of the nephron to produce
its diuretic effect?
e: Acts on the intracellular mineralocorticoid receptor and does not require access to the tubular lumen.

q: A 22-year-old man is evaluated for severe hypertension detected at a young age. His blood pressure is 174/108 mmHg on repeated measurements. His father also developed hypertension in his twenties. Laboratory investigations show:Serum K⁺: 2.8 mEq/L , Elevated serum bicarbonate, consistent with metabolic alkalosis and Normal renal function.Which of the following drugs can be used in this patient?

A pharmacologist is comparing the pharmacodynamic
properties of four experimental drugs - A, B, C, and
D - acting on the same receptor system. Their graded
dose-response curves are shown in the graph.
Based on the graph, which of the following statements
is correct?
o: B is more potent than C
C is more potent than B

q: A 58-year-old patient weighing 70 kg is administered a drug with a half-life of 3 hours and a volume of distribution of 100 mL/kg. What is the drug’s approximate clearance?
e:
In first-order kinetics, plasma half-life (T½) = 0.693 × Volume of Distribution / Clearance. Here, T½ = 3 hours = 180 minutes.
Vd = 70 × 100 = 7000 mL.
Now Clearance = 0.693 × Vd / T½ = (0.693 × 7000) / 180 = 27 mL/min.

q:
A 28-year-old pregnant woman presents with a history of taking
an over-the-counter drug for morning sickness during her first
trimester. Her baby is born with severe limb deformities, including
underdeveloped or absent long bones, giving a flipper-like
appearance to the limbs An image is given below. Which of the
following categories does the drug responsible for this condition
belong to?

A new clinical trial is conducted to evaluate a novel oral nitrate preparation in patients with a history of coronary artery disease. It is reported that the drug has a 30% bioavailability when administered orally. What does this indicate?
o: 30% of the drug is metabolized in the liver
30% of the drug is excreted unchanged in urine
30% of the drug reaches the site of action
30% of the administered dose reaches the systemic circulation in unchanged form

q:
A 60-year-old man with dyslipidemia has been taking atorvastatin for several months without any adverse effects. He develops a lower respiratory tract infection and is prescribed clarithromycin. Five days later, he presents with severe generalized myalgia, proximal muscle weakness, and dark-colored urine. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated.
Which of the following mechanisms most likely explains this drug interaction?
o: Induction of CYP3A4, causing increased metabolism of atorvastatin
Inhibition of CYP3A4, causing decreased metabolism
Induction of OATP1B1, causing increased hepatic uptake of atorvastatin
Induction of CYP2C9, causing accumulation of atorvastatin metabolites

q:
A 39-year-old commercial airline pilot presents with recurrent episodes of sneezing, nasal itching, profuse watery rhinorrhea, and itchy, watery eyes that become
particularly troublesome during the pollen season. Examination reveals pale, edematous nasal mucosa with clear nasal discharge, with no fever or evidence of respiratory infection. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate treatment for
this patient?
e: Fexofenadine is a second-generation H₁ antihistamine used for allergic rhinitis. It penetrates the CNS poorly and is described as nonsedating, making it the most appropriate choice for someone whose occupation requires continuous alertness.

q:
Histamine acting on bronchial smooth muscle produces bronchoconstriction,
whereas activation of β₂-adrenergic receptors produces relaxation of bronchial
smooth muscle and bronchodilation. Which of the following types of antagonism
is illustrated by this interaction?
e:
Histamine produces bronchoconstriction, whereas β₂-receptor activation produces
bronchodilation through a separate receptor/signaling pathway. Goodman & Gilman calls this functional antagonism; in standard pharmacology terminology, this is also called physiological antagonism

q: Which of the following antihistamines is associated with QT-interval prolongation ?

A 52-year-old man presents with recurrent attacks of severe unilateral throbbing headache lasting several hours. The headache is associated with nausea, marked
photophobia, phonophobia, and worsening with routine physical activity. Some
attacks are preceded by flashing lights in his visual field. He has a documented history of ischemic heart disease with a previous myocardial infarction. He presents during an acute attack and requires abortive therapy. Which of the following drugs can be used to manage the acute attack in this patient?
e: Lasmiditan is a selective 5-HT₁F receptor agonist approved for acute migraine treatment. It has fewer cardiovascular adverse effects than 5-HT₁B/₁D triptans and is particularly useful when cardiovascular risk factors make vasoconstrictive drugs undesirable.

q: A 24-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of severe unilateral, throbbing headache lasting several hours. The attacks are associated with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia, and the pain becomes worse with routine physical activity. He experiences these episodes frequently enough to require long-term preventive therapy. He also has a history of severe bronchial asthma with recurrent acute exacerbations requiring treatment. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate option for long-term management in this patient?
e: Divalproex is a commonly used formulation of valproate.

q:
A 63-year-old man presents with gradually progressive, painless loss of peripheral vision. Ophthalmic examination reveals elevated intraocular pressure, increased optic-disc cupping, and peripheral visual-field loss, while gonioscopy shows an open anterior chamber angle. He is started on a topical prostaglandin F₂α analogue that lowers intraocular pressure predominantly by increasing uveoscleral outflow.
Which of the following is not an adverse effect of this drug?
e: Ciliary body/muscle spasm is a muscarinic cholinergic effect, classically associated with miotic drugs such as pilocarpine. It may cause brow ache, induced myopia, and changing refraction; it is not a typical adverse effect of prostaglandin analogues

q:
A premature neonate develops tachypnea, poor feeding, failure to gain weight,
bounding peripheral pulses, and a wide pulse pressure. On cardiac examination, a continuous machinery-like murmur is heard over the left infraclavicular area.
Echocardiography demonstrates a persistent vascular connection between the
descending aorta and pulmonary artery. The pediatrician decides to attempt
pharmacological closure of this connection. Which of the following drugs can
be used in this patient?
e: Ibuprofen is a nonselective COX inhibitor that decreases prostaglandin synthesis

q: A 57-year-old woman with a chronic inflammatory arthritis presents with worsening joint pain, morning stiffness, and swelling of multiple small joints. She requires an NSAID for symptomatic relief. Her medical history is significant for peptic ulcer disease with a previous episode of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate choice in this patient?
e: Etoricoxib is a selective COX-2 inhibitor used for symptomatic relief in osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. Selective COX-2 inhibitors are less prone to cause gastric ulcers than equally effective doses of nonselective NSAIDs, making it the best option among those listed when GI toxicity is the major concern

q: A 9-year-old boy develops high-grade fever and myalgia following a viral illness. His parents give him an over-the-counter tablet repeatedly to reduce the fever. A few days later, after the fever begins to subside, he develops persistent vomiting, increasing irritability, confusion, and progressive drowsiness. He is brought to the emergency department, where examination reveals altered sensorium without focal neurological deficits. Laboratory investigations show markedly elevated liver enzymes and evidence of hepatic dysfunction. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for this condition?
e: Aspirin use during a viral febrile illness in children is associated with Reye syndrome, characterized by acute encephalopathy, liver dysfunction, and fatty infiltration of the liver and other viscera. Therefore, salicylates are contraindicated in children and young adults with viral illness-associated fever.

q:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after
intentionally ingesting a large number of paracetamol tablets in a self-harm attempt. She complains of nausea and upper abdominal discomfort. The treating physician
identifies the overdose and starts N-acetylcysteine promptly. What is the principal mechanism of action of this antidote?
e: In paracetamol overdose, hepatic glutathione becomes depleted, allowing the toxic metabolite NAPQI to accumulate. NAC replenishes glutathione stores and can also serve as a glutathione substitute to detoxify NAPQI.

q:
A 64-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe pain, redness, warmth, and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The pain began overnight and is so intense that even the touch of a bedsheet is unbearable. Arthrocentesis shows needle
-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. He also has severe chronic kidney dysfunction with markedly reduced eGFR. The physician wants to treat the acute inflammatory
attack. Which of the following drugs can be used in this patient?
e: Glucocorticoids are among the standard anti-inflammatory treatments for an acute gout flare. In a patient with severe renal dysfunction and involvement of a limited number of joints, an intra-articular glucocorticoid avoids the renal toxicity associated with NSAIDs.

q:
A 49-year-old man presents with sudden severe pain, redness, warmth, and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Joint fluid examination reveals needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. He is prescribed colchicine to control the acute inflammatory attack. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of
action of this drug?
e: Colchicine binds to tubulin and interferes with microtubule formation/depolymerizes microtubules, thereby reducing neutrophil migration, adhesion, and recruitment to the inflamed joint.

q:
A 19-year-old boy with a high-burden hematological malignancy is started on intensive chemotherapy. Within 24 hours, he develops nausea, repeated vomiting, painful muscle cramps, generalized weakness, perioral tingling, and decreased urine output. ECG shows rhythm abnormalities. Laboratory investigations reveal marked hyperkalemia,
hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, and rising serum creatinine. The treating team decides to administer a drug that can rapidly reduce the already elevated serum uric acid level.Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Inhibition of OAT/URAT-1, increasing uric acid excretion
e: Rasburicase is a recombinant uricase used in malignancy-associated hyperuricemia. It oxidizes uric acid to allantoin, a more soluble and inactive metabolite, and can reduce uric acid levels within hours.

q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman with rheumatoid arthritis has persistent symmetrical pain and swelling involving the small joints of both hands, associated with prolonged morning stiffness. Because treatment is required during pregnancy, she is started on a 4-aminoquinoline disease-modifying drug. This drug is also known for extensive tissue sequestration and a very large apparent volume of distribution.During follow-up, the physician counsels her regarding important adverse effects associated with long- term therapy.Which of the following adverse effects is not associated with this drug?
o: Reactivation of tuberculosis and hepatitis B
e: Reactivation of latent TB or HBV is not a characteristic adverse effect of chloroquine/ hydroxychloroquine; this concern is much more typical of potent biologic immunosuppressive therapy like infliximab

q:
A patient with bronchial asthma is prescribed an additional
drug for symptomatic control of respiratory symptoms. The
site of action of the drug is marked in the diagram given
below . Which of the following drugs was most likely
prescribed?

A 27-year-old woman with a long-standing history of bronchial asthma is receiving regular high-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus a long-acting β₂ agonist (LABA). Despite good compliance and correct inhaler technique, she continues to experience recurrent exacerbations, particularly during the pollen season. She also has associated seasonal allergic rhinitis. Between exacerbations, spirometry shows near-normal lung function. Allergy evaluation demonstrates sensitization to aeroallergens with elevated serum IgE levels. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
e: Omalizumab is a humanized anti-IgE monoclonal antibody used in severe allergic asthma. It binds circulating IgE and prevents its interaction with high-affinity IgE receptors on mast cells, thereby reducing allergen-induced activation and asthma exacerbations. Goodman & Gilman also notes that omalizumab can be particularly effective in preventing seasonal exacerbations.

q:
A 16-year-old boy with persistent bronchial asthma is using beclomethasone through a pressurized metered-dose inhaler (pMDI). During follow-up, he reports difficulty synchronizing inhaler actuation with inspiration and has developed recurrent
hoarseness and oral candidiasis. His physician advises attaching a spacer to the inhaler. Which of the following best describes the effect of adding a spacer device?
o: It increases deposition of the drug in the oropharynx and systemic absorption
It reduces oropharyngeal deposition and increases the proportion of drug reaching the lower airways
It requires a higher inspiratory flow for effective drug delivery
It converts the aerosolized drug into a dry-powder formulation
e: A large-volume spacer reduces the velocity of aerosol particles, allows some propellant evaporation, decreases impaction in the oropharynx, and increases the proportion of drug inhaled into the lower airways. It is particularly useful for reducing local adverse effects of inhaled corticosteroids.

q:
A 41-year-old woman presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and
occasional presyncope for the past several months. Examination reveals a prominent P2 and right ventricular heave. Echocardiography suggests markedly elevated
pulmonary artery pressure, and right-heart catheterization confirms pulmonary arterial hypertension. The physician decides to start an oral endothelin receptor antagonist that preferentially blocks the ETA receptor while largely sparing the ETB receptor.
Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?
e: Ambrisentan is a relatively selective ETA receptor antagonist, with approximately 4000-fold greater affinity for ETA than ETB receptors.

q: A 46-year-old man presents with a productive cough with thick, tenacious sputum that is difficult to expectorate. The physician prescribes N-acetylcysteine. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Breaks disulfide bonds in mucus glycoproteins
e:
N-acetylcysteine reduces mucus viscosity by breaking disulfide bonds in mucoproteins/mucus glycoproteins, making sputum easier to clear.
Golden Points
N-acetylcysteine → mucolytic → breaks disulfide bonds → ↓ mucus viscosity.
N-acetylcysteine is also the antidote for paracetamol toxicity because it replenishes glutathione stores. Ambroxol/Bromhexine → depolymerization of mucopolysaccharides + improved mucociliary clearance

q: A 61-year-old man with chronic stable angina has been using a transdermal nitroglycerin patch continuously throughout the day and night for several weeks. Initially, his exertional chest pain was well controlled, but he gradually notices that the same dose produces significantly less symptomatic relief despite good compliance. The physician explains that prolonged continuous exposure has resulted in tolerance to the drug. Which of the following best explains the development of this tolerance?
o: Increased expression of soluble guanylyl cyclase with increased cGMP formation
Depletion of cellular sulfhydryl groups along with inactivation of mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 (ALDH2), resulting in reduced nitrate bioactivation
Increased sensitivity of vascular smooth muscle to nitric oxide
Inhibition of phosphodiesterase-5 leading to excessive degradation of cGMP
e: Goodman & Gilman identifies cellular sulfhydryl depletion and ALDH2 inactivation among the mechanisms implicated in nitrate tolerance. Reduced ability to bioactivate nitroglycerin results in diminished NO-mediated vasodilation.

q: A 58-year-old man is admitted with a hypertensive emergency. His blood pressure is 238/142 mmHg, and he has severe breathlessness, bilateral basal crepitations, and radiological evidence of pulmonary edema. He is started on a continuous intravenous infusion of a rapid-acting vasodilator that releases nitric oxide and reduces both preload and afterload. Because adequate blood-pressure control is difficult, the infusion is continued at a relatively high rate. Several hours later, the patient develops restlessness, confusion, tachypnea, cardiovascular instability, and severe unexplained lactic acidosis despite adequate oxygenation. Toxicity from a metabolite of the antihypertensive drug is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate antidote?
e: The drug being infused is sodium nitroprusside. Its metabolism releases cyanide, and excessive or prolonged high-dose administration can cause cyanide accumulation with severe lactic aci- dosis. Goodman & Gilman lists hydroxocobalamin as an antidote for cyanide poisoning.

q: A 62-year-old man with ischemic heart disease and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is receiving metoprolol for ventricular rate control. His resting heart rate is 58/min. On repeated follow-up visits, his blood pressure remains elevated at 164/96 mmHg, and the physician plans to add another antihypertensive drug. Which of the following drugs should not be added to his current therapy?
e: Both verapamil and β-blockers depress heart rate and AV nodal conduction. Their combination can produce severe bradycardia, AV block, and depression of left ventricular function and should therefore be avoided.

q: A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is found to have persistent hypertension and significant albuminuria on repeated testing. He was previously unable to tolerate an ACE inhibitor because of persistent dry cough. The physician starts telmisartan, which selectively blocks the AT₁ receptor for angiotensin II. Which of the following best describes the principal hemodynamic mechanism by which this drug lowers blood pressure?
o: Increases peripheral vascular resistance and increases afterload
Decreases peripheral vascular resistance and decreases afterload
Decreases the amount of blood returning to the heart and decreases preload
e: Telmisartan blocks AT₁-mediated vasoconstriction, resulting in vasodilation and a decrease in total peripheral vascular resistance, which lowers arterial pressure and afterload.

q: A 61-year-old woman with hypertension is taking telmisartan, amlodipine, and chlorthalidone at maximally tolerated doses. Her medication adherence is confirmed, and ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring shows an average BP of 166/98 mmHg. Evaluation does not reveal a secondary cause of hypertension, and her renal function and serum potassium are within acceptable limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug to add for better blood-pressure control?
e: Persistent hypertension despite an ARB + calcium-channel blocker + thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic represents resistant hypertension.

q: A 63-year-old man with chronic stable angina has been taking long-acting nitrates and uses sublingual nitroglycerin when required for chest discomfort. Without informing his physician, he purchases sildenafil over the counter for erectile dysfunction.A few hours after taking sildenafil, he develops marked dizziness, profound weakness, and near-syncope. On arrival at the emergency department, he is pale and diaphoretic, with a blood pressure of 72/44 mmHg. There is no evidence of acute bleeding or a new myocardial infarction. What is the most likely explanation for his acute deterioration?
o: Vasodilatory shock due to excessive cGMP-mediated vasodilation
Cardiogenic shock due to direct myocardial depression by sildenafil
Rebound hypertension due to development of nitrate tolerance
Acute coronary vasospasm caused by inhibition of PDE5
e: Organic nitrates increase NO-mediated cGMP formation, whereas sildenafil inhibits PDE5-mediated breakdown of cGMP. When given together, they act synergistically, producing a profound increase in cGMP and a dramatic fall in blood pressure. This is why PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated in patients receiving nitrates.

q: A 29-year-old woman with a history of chronic hypertension comes for follow-up after discovering that she is 8 weeks pregnant. Her blood pressure is 154/96 mmHg on repeated measurements. She has no proteinuria, no evidence of end-organ dysfunction, and requires continued antihypertensive treatment during pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate antihypertensive drug for this patient?
e: Methyldopa is specifically described as a preferred drug for treatment of hypertension during pregnancy, based on effectiveness and safety for both mother and fetus.

q: A 67-year-old man presents with progressively worsening exertional dyspnea, marked fatigue, orthopnea, and episodes of breathlessness that awaken him from sleep. Examination reveals elevated JVP, bilateral basal crepitations, an S3 gallop, and bilateral pitting pedal edema. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 28%. Several drugs are being considered as part of his long-term pharmacological management. Which of the following drugs doesn’t reduce its overall mortality ?

A 66-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, easy fatigability, and bilateral pedal edema. Examination reveals elevated JVP, bilateral basal crepitations, and an S3 gallop. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. The physician decides to add a drug that inhibits sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) in the renal tubule, reducing glucose reabsorption and increasing urinary glucose excretion. Which of the following drugs has this mechanism of action?
e: Dapagliflozin is an SGLT2 inhibitor that decreases renal glucose reabsorption and increases glucose excretion. Goodman & Gilman specifically states that SGLT2 inhibitors are beneficial in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, even in patients without diabetes.

q: A 64-year-old man with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is receiving long-term therapy that includes a β-blocker. He is admitted with an acute anterior-wall myocardial infarction. Over the next several hours, he develops severe breathlessness, cold clammy extremities, confusion, and markedly reduced urine output. His blood pressure falls to 76/46 mmHg, and echocardiography shows severe global left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 18%. After initial stabilization of his blood pressure, he continues to have evidence of markedly reduced cardiac output. An intravenous positive inotrope is required. Because he is already receiving a β-blocker, the physician prefers an agent whose inotropic action does not depend on β-adrenergic receptor stimulation. But increases CAMP by inhibiting PDE. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?
e: Milrinone inhibits cardiac PDE3/PDE4, decreases cAMP degradation, and increases intracellular cAMP independently of β-receptor activation. Goodman & Gilman specifically states that PDE inhibitors may be advantageous in patients receiving β-blockers

q: A 56-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of palpitations, fatigue, and exertional breathlessness. ECG during an episode shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with absent discrete P waves. He also has left ventricular systolic dysfunction. For ventricular rate control, he is started on digoxin. Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Blockade of fast voltage- gated Na⁺ channels
Blockade of delayed rectifier K⁺ channels

q: A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation and chronic heart failure has been receiving digoxin for several months. He presents with nausea, loss of appetite, confusion, and yellowish discoloration of vision. ECG shows frequent premature ventricular complexes with ventricular bigeminy. Serum digoxin concentration is elevated, and the offending drug is stopped. There is no severe hyperkalemia or hemodynamic instability. Which of the following antiarrhythmic drugs can be used to control the ventricular arrhythmia in this patient?
e: Lidocaine is a Class IB Na⁺-channel blocker used intravenously for acute ventricular arrhythmias.

q: A 59-year-old man with chronic stable angina continues to experience episodes of retrosternal chest discomfort during exertion despite receiving standard antianginal therapy. His physician adds a second-line antianginal drug, ranolazine.Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Inhibition of the late inward Na⁺ current
e: Ranolazine inhibits the late inward Na⁺ current (late INa) is thought to account for its important cardiac effects. This reduces intracellular Na⁺ and secondary Ca²⁺ overload during ischemia.

q: A 65-year-old man with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is receiving guideline- directed medical therapy. He was recently hospitalized because of worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, peripheral edema, and pulmonary congestion. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 30%. Despite optimization of his existing treatment, he remains symptomatic, so the physician adds vericiguat. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of vericiguat?
o: Blocks the funny (If) current through HCN channels
Directly stimulates soluble guanylyl cyclase and sensitizes it to endogenous nitric oxide
Inhibits neprilysin and increases endogenous natriuretic peptides
Inhibits phosphodiesterase-3 and increases intracellular cAMP

q: A 63-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy has recurrent episodes of sustained ventricular tachycardia despite previous therapy. He is started on long-term amiodarone to prevent recurrence. During follow-up, the physician counsels him regarding toxicities that may occur because the drug accumulates extensively in tissues and has a very long elimination half-life. Which of the following is not  a typical adverse effect of long-term amiodarone therapy?

A 52-year-old man with dyslipidemia is started on a cholesterol-lowering
medication. Soon after taking the drug, he develops intense warmth,
redness, and flushing of the face and upper trunk, similar to the appearance
shown in the image below. He has no difficulty breathing or features of an
allergic reaction Which of the following medications is most likely
responsible for this presentation?
e: Niacin commonly produces flushing and pruritus of the face and upper trunk. The flushing is prostaglandin-mediated, particularly through release of PGD₂ from the skin.

q: A 31-year-old woman with dyslipidemia and persistently elevated LDL cholesterol is found to be 10 weeks pregnant. She requires lipid-lowering therapy, and the physician wants to choose an agent that lowers LDL cholesterol but has minimal systemic exposure because it is not absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate choice?
e: Colesevelam is a bile acid sequestrant. These agents are considered among the safest lipid-lowering drugs because they are not absorbed systemically. They bind bile acids in the intestine, increase their fecal excretion, increase hepatic LDL-receptor expression, and thereby lower LDL-C

q: A 54-year-old man with newly diagnosed essential hypertension is started on a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker. During follow-up, the physician wants to choose an agent that produces effective arterial vasodilation but is least likely to produce reflex tachycardia because, in addition to blocking vascular L-type Ca²⁺ channels, it also blocks N-type Ca²⁺ channels on sympathetic nerve terminals, thereby reducing norepinephrine release. Which of the following drugs has this property?
e: Cilnidipine blocks both L-type and N-type Ca²⁺ channels. N-type channel blockade decreases sympathetic norepinephrine release, which helps blunt the reflex sympathetic response and makes reflex tachycardia less likely than with conventional L-type dihydropyridines.

q: A 48-year-old woman with a nonmyeloid malignancy is receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy. After several treatment cycles, she develops easy bruising, petechiae, and prolonged bleeding from venipuncture sites. Her platelet count is 18,000/µL, while the physician attributes the thrombocytopenia to chemotherapy-induced bone-marrow suppression. The oncologist wants to use a hematopoietic growth factor that specifically promotes megakaryocyte maturation and increases platelet production. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate?
e: Oprelvekin is recombinant IL-11. It promotes megakaryocyte maturation and produces a thrombopoietic response.

q: A 24-year-old woman presents with easy fatigability, exertional breathlessness, palpitations, and pica. Examination shows pallor. Laboratory investigations reveal low hemoglobin, microcytic hypochromic red cells, low serum ferritin, and increased total iron-binding capacity. She is started on oral ferrous sulfate. The physician considers adding another agent to increase the intestinal absorption and improve the efficacy of oral iron therapy. Which of the following should be co-administered?

A 67-year-old man with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation is started on apixaban to reduce the risk of thromboembolic stroke. During a teaching discussion, the resident is asked about the mechanism of action of this anticoagulant. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of apixaban?
o: Indirect factor Xa inhibitor through antithrombin activation

q: A 72-year-old man with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation has been receiving an oral direct thrombin ( IIa) inhibitor for prevention of thromboembolic stroke. He is brought to the emergency department with hematemesis, melena, dizziness, and hypotension. Laboratory evaluation suggests significant ongoing anticoagulant effect, and urgent reversal is required. Which of the following is the specific antidote for this patient?
e: The oral direct factor IIa inhibitor in the question is dabigatran. Idarucizumab is a humanized Fab fragment that binds dabigatran with very high affinity and rapidly reverses its anticoagulant effect.

q: A 32-year-old man with generalized anxiety disorder was recently prescribed alprazolam. He is brought to the emergency department after accidentally consuming several tablets at once. He is markedly drowsy, has slurred speech, impaired coordination, and depressed consciousness, but remains hemodynamically stable. Which of the following can be used to reverse the effects of this drug overdose?
e: Alprazolam is a benzodiazepine. Flumazenil competitively antagonizes the benzodiazepine binding site on the GABA A receptor and is indicated for reversal of benzodiazepine overdose.

q: A 9-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent jaundice with persistent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Liver enzymes are otherwise normal, and investigations show markedly reduced, but not completely absent, bilirubin glucuronidation due to deficient UGT1A1 activity. He is diagnosed with Crigler–Najjar syndrome type IIThe physician decides to start a drug that can induce UGT1A1 expression and thereby increase . bilirubin glucuronidation and elimination. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate?
e: Phenobarbital induces UGT1A1 gene expression, improving the glucuronidation and elimination of bilirubin in patients with Crigler–Najjar syndrome type II.

q: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after suddenly developing generalized tonic stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking of all four limbs. The episode lasts for approximately 2 minutes. After the convulsive movements stop, he does not regain consciousness, and within a few minutes he develops another generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He remains unresponsive between the two episodes. IV access is established and the treating team wants to rapidly terminate the ongoing seizure activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?
e: IV lorazepam is an effective benzodiazepine for rapidly terminating status epilepticus. Goodman & Gilman notes that both lorazepam and diazepam have established roles, but lorazepam is used more frequently because diazepam has a shorter duration of antiseizure action.

q: A 10-year-old child with a history of generalized seizures is receiving antiseizure therapy. A few weeks after starting treatment, he develops fever with a widespread erythematous rash and painful mucocutaneous lesions. Because of concern for a serious drug-induced cutaneous reaction, the treating physician wants to select an antiseizure drug that is least associated with significant skin rash among the following options. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate choice?
e: Clobazam is a benzodiazepine used in several seizure phenotypes. Goodman & Gilman lists its characteristic adverse effects as somnolence and sedation, without rash being highlighted among its characteristic toxicities, making it the best choice among these options when signifi- cant cutaneous reactions are the concern.

q: A 58-year-old man with long-standing diabetes mellitus presents with burning pain, tingling, and an electric-shock-like sensation in both feet, which is worse at night. Examination reveals reduced distal sensation. He is diagnosed with painful peripheral neuropathy and is started on gabapentin. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Binding to the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
Direct activation of GABA A receptors
e: Gabapentin binds with high affinity to the α2δ-1 subunit of voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, reducing neuronal Ca²⁺ currents and neuronal excitability.

q: A 7-month-old infant is brought by his parents for recurrent clusters of sudden flexion of the neck, trunk, and limbs, particularly after awakening. Examination reveals multiple hypopigmented “ash-leaf” macules over the trunk. MRI brain shows findings consistent with tuberous sclerosis complex, and EEG demonstrates hypsarrhythmia. Which of the following drugs is particularly useful for the treatment of these infantile spasms?
e: Vigabatrin is especially useful for infantile spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis. It irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase, increasing GABA concentrations in the brain.

q: A 62-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia has been receiving antipsychotic therapy for several years. Her psychiatric symptoms are stable, but her relatives recently notice repetitive chewing and lip-puckering movements, protrusion of the tongue, facial grimacing, and irregular choreiform movements of her fingers and upper limbs. She has no fever, marked rigidity, or altered consciousness. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for this adverse effect?
e: The clinical picture represents tardive dyskinesia, which occurs after months or years of dopa- mine-blocking therapy and manifests with orofacial dyskinesia, choreiform movements, and stereotypies. Risk increases with the potency of D₂ blockade; haloperidol is a high-potency first-generation D₂ antagonist.

q: A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia is being treated with haloperidol. Several days after an increase in dose, he develops high-grade fever, severe generalized muscle rigidity, altered consciousness, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and markedly labile blood pressure. Laboratory investigations reveal a markedly elevated serum creatine kinase level and myoglobinuria. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
o: Continue the typical antipsychotic and administer bromocriptine
Stop the typical antipsychotic and administer bromocriptine
Stop the typical antipsychotic and administer benztropine
Continue the typical antipsychotic and administer dantrolene
e: The presentation is characteristic of neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). It requires immediate cessation of the antipsychotic, supportive care, and pharmacological treatment with a dopamine agonist such as bromocriptine

q: A 25-year-old man with newly diagnosed schizophrenia presents with persistent auditory hallucinations, suspiciousness, social withdrawal, and reduced emotional expression. He previously developed marked rigidity and tremor during a short trial of a potent D₂-blocking antipsychotic. He is also overweight and has a strong family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. His psychiatrist therefore wants an antipsychotic effective for schizophrenia with a relatively low risk of extrapyramidal and metabolic adverse effects. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?
e: Aripiprazole is a partial D₂ receptor agonist. Its intrinsic dopaminergic activity helps maintain signaling below the threshold associated with prominent EPS, and it is also among the more metabolically benign antipsychotics.

q: 42-year-old woman with bipolar disorder has been receiving lithium maintenance therapy for the past 3 years. Her mood symptoms remain well controlled, and her serum lithium concentration is within the therapeutic range. During follow-up, the physician discusses adverse effects that may occur with prolonged lithium therapy. Which of the following statements about lithium is not correct?
o: Lithium can cause tremors at normal therapeutic plasma concentrations
Lithium can cause T wave depression

q: A 38-year-old woman with major depressive disorder that has responded poorly to multiple antidepressants is started on a different antidepressant. A few weeks later, she attends a dinner party and consumes red wine and aged cheese. Within a short time, she develops a severe throbbing headache, palpitations, diaphoresis, nausea, and marked elevation of blood pressure to 210/120 mmHg. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for this reaction?
e: Phenelzine is an irreversible nonselective MAO-A and MAO-B inhibitor. Inhibition of gastrointestinal and hepatic MAO allows dietary tyramine from foods such as red wine and aged cheese to reach the systemic circulation, causing a large release of norepinephrine and potentially a severe hypertensive crisis.

q: A 32-year-old woman with major depressive disorder has been receiving amitriptyline. She is brought to the emergency department after an intentional overdose of her medication. She is drowsy and hypotensive, with dry mouth, dilated pupils, tachycardia, and an ECG showing marked QRS widening. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for  this overdose?

A 39-year-old woman presents with persistent depressed mood, loss of interest, low energy, impaired concentration, and reduced productivity for the past 4 months. She also smokes nearly one pack of cigarettes daily and has made several unsuccessful attempts to quit. She now wants pharmacological treatment for her depression and would prefer a medication that may also help her stop smoking. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?

A 68-year-old man with Parkinson disease has been receiving levodopa for bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor. Despite therapy, he continues to have significant
parkinsonian symptoms. The physician decides to add carbidopa to his treatment
regimen. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of carbidopa?
o: Inhibits both central and peripheral DOPA decarboxylase
e: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC/DOPA decarboxylase). This reduces the peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine and increases the fraction of levodopa available to reach the CNS.

q: A 72-year-old man is brought by his family with progressive memory loss, increasing disorientation, difficulty recognizing familiar places, and inability to independently manage routine daily activities. His cognitive decline has gradually worsened over the past few years, and he is diagnosed with Alzheimer disease. The physician decides to start a drug that acts by blocking NMDA-type glutamate receptors and reducing excitotoxic neuronal injury. Which of the following drugs is being described?
e: Memantine is an uncompetitive antagonist of the NMDA-type glutamate receptor. It reduces pathological NMDA receptor activation and excitotoxicity and is indicated particularly for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer dementia.

q:
A 28-year-old man is brought unconscious after ingesting an unknown drug. On
examination, he has markedly constricted pinpoint pupils and severe respiratory
depression with a very low respiratory rate. He is unresponsive to verbal commands. Which of the following drugs can be used in this patient?
e: The combination of coma + pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression strongly suggests opioid poisoning. Naloxone is an opioid receptor antagonist that rapidly reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression.

q: A 60-year-old man undergoes partial small-bowel resection with primary anastomosis. In the postoperative period, he develops progressive abdominal distension, nausea, inability to tolerate oral feeds, failure to pass flatus, and hypoactive bowel sounds suggesting post operative ileus. Abdominal imaging does not show any evidence of a mechanical obstruction. Which of the following drugs can be used to accelerate gastrointestinal recovery in this patient?

A 45-year-old man with alcohol dependence is receiving pharmacological therapy as part of an abstinence program. During a celebration, he consumes alcohol and within minutes develops marked facial flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, sweating, dizziness, hypotension, and near-syncope.The reaction is due to the drug he is taking. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Enhancement of GABA A receptor activity
e: The clinical picture represents a disulfiram–alcohol reaction. Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH), causing a marked rise in acetaldehyde after alcohol consumption. Accumulated acetaldehyde produces flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, hypotension, and syncope.

q: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus has been taking glibenclamide for the past 2 years, with good glycemic control. He is subsequently diagnosed with hypertriglyceridemia and is started on gemfibrozil. One week later, he begins experiencing recurrent episodes of profuse sweating, palpitations, tremulousness, confusion, and dizziness. During one such episode, his blood glucose is found to be markedly reduced. Which of the following best explains this?
o: Inhibition of CYP mediated metabolism of glibenclamide by gemfibrozil
Displacement of glibenclamide from plasma protein-binding sites by gemfibrozil
Increased renal excretion of glibenclamide by gemfibrozil
Decreased gastrointestinal absorption of glibenclamide by gemfibrozil
e: A Reduced hepatic metabolism increases exposure to the sulfonylurea, thereby potentiating its glucose-lowering effect and increasing the risk of hypoglycemia.

q: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus for the past 10 years presents for optimization of her glucose-lowering therapy. During history taking, she reports three episodes of vulvovaginal candidiasis over the previous 2 years, characterized by recurrent vulvar itching and thick vaginal discharge requiring antifungal treatment. Her physician wants to avoid an antidiabetic drug that could predispose her to further genital mycotic infections. Which of the following drugs should be avoided in this patient?

A 55-year-old woman with estrogen receptor–positive breast carcinoma undergoes
surgical treatment and is subsequently started on tamoxifen as long-term adjuvant hormonal therapy. During follow-up, she is counseled regarding important adverse effects related to the partial estrogen-agonist action of tamoxifen on the uterus. Which of the following is the most significant adverse effect associated with
tamoxifen therapy?

An 11-year-old boy is evaluated for severe proportionate short stature and markedly reduced growth velocity since early childhood. His parents are of normal height. Examination shows increased subcutaneous fat and reduced muscle development,
while his intellectual development is normal. Laboratory evaluation reveals elevated serum growth hormone with markedly reduced IGF-1 levels and previous treatment
with recombinant growth hormone has produced little improvement. Which of the
following classes of drugs is most appropriate for this patient?

A 48-year-old man presents with progressive enlargement of the hands and feet,
coarse facial features, increased sweating, headaches, and widening of the spaces between his teeth. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated growth hormone and IGF-1 levels, and MRI reveals a pituitary adenoma. He undergoes transsphenoidal surgery, but biochemical abnormalities persist. He is subsequently treated with octreotide, yet his symptoms and elevated IGF-1 levels remain inadequately controlled. Which of the following drugs can be used in this patient?
e: Pegvisomant is a growth hormone receptor antagonist approved for acromegaly. It binds the GH receptor but prevents the conformational change required for JAK-STAT signaling and IGF-1 production. Goodman & Gilman specifically states that pegvisomant may be added when IGF-1 remains inadequately controlled with somatostatin analogues.

q: A 46-year-old man with obesity is started on orlistat as part of a weight-reduction program. A few weeks after beginning therapy, he complains of steatorrhea, increased frequency of defecation, fecal urgency, flatulence with oily discharge, and abdominal discomfort. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of orlistat?
o: GLP-1 receptor agonism leading to reduced food intake and delayed gastric emptying
Inhibition of gastric and pancreatic lipases, thereby decreasing dietary fat absorption
Activation of central 5-HT₂C receptors to promote satiety
Increased release of norepinephrine in the CNS resulting in appetite suppression
e: Orlistat inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases, preventing hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides into absorbable fatty acids. Reduced fat absorption accounts for its weight-loss effect and its characteristic gastrointestinal adverse effects, including steatorrhea, fecal urgency, and oily discharge.

q: A 29-year-old woman presents with amenorrhea, infertility, and spontaneous milky discharge from both breasts for the past 6 months. Pregnancy testing is negative. Laboratory evaluation reveals a markedly elevated serum prolactin concentration, and MRI of the pituitary shows a small prolactin-secreting adenoma. Which of the following drugs is the preferred pharmacological treatment for this patient?
e: Cabergoline is a long-acting dopamine D₂ receptor agonist that suppresses prolactin secretion and reduces prolactinoma size. It is the preferred drug for hyperprolactinemia because of its greater efficacy and better tolerability compared with bromocriptine.

q:
A 67-year-old postmenopausal woman is diagnosed with osteoporosis after bone
mineral density testing shows a markedly reduced T-score. Her physician prescribes an oral medication and instructs her to take it with a full glass of water, at least 30 minutes before breakfast, and to remain upright after taking the tablet.
Which of the following drugs has most likely been prescribed?
e: Alendronate is an oral bisphosphonate. Oral bisphosphonates have poor gastrointestinal absorption and should be taken with a full glass of water and at least 30 minutes before breakfast. Remaining upright helps reduce esophageal irritation and esophagitis

q: A 68-year-old man presents with progressive difficulty initiating urination, a weak urinary stream, straining during micturition, nocturia, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. Digital rectal examination reveals a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate, and evaluation is consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia.The physician wants to prescribe a drug that can reduce the size of the enlarged prostate . Which of the following mechanisms of action would be most appropriate?
o: Continuous administration of a GnRH agonist
e: Finasteride and dutasteride inhibit the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and can reduce prostate volume. Their clinical effect develops gradually over several months. Continuous GnRH agonist administration — Incorrect: Chronic GnRH agonist therapy eventually suppresses LH and testosterone through pituitary GnRH-receptor downregulation, but Goodman & Gilman discusses this approach as androgen-deprivation therapy for prostate cancer, not routine treatment of BPH.

q:
A 44-year-old man presents with recurrent burning epigastric discomfort, nausea, and upper abdominal pain. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals mucosal
ulceration in the proximal duodenum. Gastric biopsy testing is positive for
Helicobacter pylori. Which of the following represents the standard triple-drug
regimen for eradication of this infection?

A 35-year-old woman is prescribed a dopamine D₂ receptor–blocking prokinetic
drug for persistent nausea and impaired gastric emptying. During discussion of
the adverse-effect profiles of metoclopramide and domperidone, the physician
makes the following statements. Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Domperidone does not readily cause extrapyramidal symptoms
e: can increase prolactin levels and may produce galactorrhea, gynecomastia, amenorrhea, or impotence.

q:
A 54-year-old woman with breast carcinoma is scheduled to receive a highly emetogenic chemotherapy regimen. During her previous chemotherapy cycle, she developed severe nausea and repeated vomiting within the first 24 hours, followed by persistent nausea and vomiting over the next 2 days. For the next cycle, her oncologist plans a
combination regimen that provides protection against both the acute and delayed
phases of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Which of the following drug
combinations is most appropriate?
e: Granisetron is a 5-HT₃ receptor antagonist, while aprepitant is an NK₁ receptor antagonist. Goodman & Gilman states that aprepitant is typically administered together with a 5-HT₃ antagonist and dexamethasone for moderately or highly emetogenic chemotherapy

q:
A 41-year-old man presents with recurrent retrosternal burning, sour-tasting
regurgitation, and worsening of symptoms after meals and while lying down. He
also complains of postprandial fullness. The physician considers adding a prokinetic agent that increases lower esophageal sphincter tone and promotes gastric emptying. Which of the following drugs has this pharmacological action?
e: Metoclopramide has prokinetic and antiemetic actions. By antagonizing D₂ receptors in the gastrointestinal tract, it facilitates acetylcholine release, thereby increasing GI motility, promoting gastric emptying, and increasing lower esophageal sphincter tone.

q: A 66-year-old man presents with fever, dysuria, urinary frequency, and right-sided flank pain. Urine culture grows a gram-negative bacillus, and he is started on an oral antibiotic. His urinary symptoms improve over the next few days. One week after starting treatment, he develops sudden pain and swelling over the back of his ankle, with marked tenderness along the Achilles tendon and difficulty walking. There is no history of trauma. The physician suspects that this musculoskeletal problem is an adverse effect of the recently prescribed antimicrobial drug. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the drug responsible for this adverse effect?
o: Inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal subunit
Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis
Inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis
e: The patient has developed Achilles tendinitis associated with a fluoroquinolone. Quinolones inhibit the bacterial type II topoisomerases DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, thereby interfering with bacterial DNA replication. Goodman & Gilman identifies tendinitis and tendon rupture, particularly involving the Achilles tendon, as a serious adverse effect of fluoroquinolones.

q:
A 46-year-old woman presents with high-grade fever, chills, burning micturition, increased urinary frequency, right-sided flank pain, and costovertebral-angle
tenderness. Urinalysis shows pyuria and positive nitrites, suggesting an urinary tract infection. She has a history of an immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin and also has pre-existing hearing impairment. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug among the given options?
e: Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone. Goodman & Gilman states that fluoroquinolones are useful for upper and lower UTIs, including pyelonephritis, making ciprofloxacin the most appropriate choice among these options.

q:
A 64-year-old man is admitted with high-grade fever, dysuria, urinary frequency, and flank pain. Urine culture grows a gram-negative bacillus susceptible to β-lactam therapy. His medical records show that he previously developed generalized urticaria,
bronchospasm, and hypotension immediately after receiving penicillin, consistent with a severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?
e: Aztreonam is a monobactam β-lactam antibiotic active only against gram-negative organisms, including Pseudomonas. Goodman & Gilman specifically states that it has a notable lack of allergic cross-reactivity with other β-lactams and is useful for gram-negative infections in patients with severe hypersensitivity reactions to other β-lactam classes.

q: A 46-year-old man presents with high-grade fever, chills, malaise, and progressive shortness of breath. Examination reveals a new systolic murmur, and multiple blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase-positive and coagulase- positive. Echocardiography demonstrates a vegetation on the mitral valve. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing shows that the isolate is susceptible to methicillin-class β-lactam antibiotics. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for this patient?
e: The findings indicate Staphylococcus aureus that remains susceptible to methicillin. Goodman & Gilman states that penicillinase-resistant penicillins such as oxacillin are preferred for S. aureus that is not methicillin resistant and specifically describes high-dose IV oxacillin for serious infections such as endocarditis.

q:
A 38-year-old man with a past history of generalized tonic-clonic seizures, currently well controlled on antiseizure therapy, develops a bacterial infection requiring antimicrobial treatment. Because of his seizure history, the physician wants to choose an antimicrobial that is least likely to lower the seizure threshold or precipitate convulsions.
Which of the following antimicrobial drugs is least likely to cause seizures?

A 26-year-old woman who is 22 weeks pregnant presents to the clinic after her
husband is admitted with confirmed meningococcal meningitis caused by Neisseria
meningitidis. She has had prolonged close household contact with him and is currently asymptomatic. Because of the significant risk of secondary meningococcal disease among close contacts, the physician decides to provide post-exposure
chemoprophylaxis. Which of the following is the most appropriate chemoprophylactic drug for this pregnant woman?

A 38-year-old man presents with chronic cough, low-grade fever, night sweats, loss of appetite, and progressive weight loss. Sputum testing detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and molecular drug- susceptibility testing demonstrates resistance to both isoniazid and rifampicin. The patient is considered for the newer 6-month all-oral BPaLM regimen. What is the mechanism of action of the “Pa” component of this regimen?
e: Pretomanid inhibits M. tuberculosis mycolic acid and protein synthesis under aerobic conditions. In nonreplicating organisms, it additionally generates reactive nitrogen species and can cause ATP depletion.

q: A 36-year-old man presents with persistent cough, low-grade fever, night sweats, loss of appetite, and progressive weight loss for the past several weeks. Sputum testing confirms Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and drug-susceptibility testing shows drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis. He is started on the standard first-line regimen under directly observed therapy. After several weeks of treatment, he develops progressive blurring of vision, reduced visual acuity, and difficulty distinguishing red from green colors. Which of the following antitubercular drugs is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
e: The most important adverse effect of ethambutol is optic neuritis, producing decreased visual acuity and loss of red-green color discrimination. The risk is related to dose and duration of therapy.

q:
A 38-year-old man presents with fever, chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and loss of appetite. Sputum examination confirms pulmonary tuberculosis. Further
evaluation reveals that he is HIV-positive with a CD4 count of 35 cells/mm³. He has no features suggestive of tuberculous meningitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate sequence of treatment?
o: Start A first, followed by ART within 2 weeks
Start ART first, followed by ATT after 2 weeks
Start ATT and ART simultaneously on the same day
Complete the entire course of ATT before starting ART
e: In HIV-associated active TB with CD4 <50 cells/mm³ and no TB meningitis, TB treatment is started first and ART is initiated as soon as possible, within 2 weeks.

q:
A 32-year-old woman with borderline tuberculoid leprosy has been receiving regular multidrug therapy for the past 3 months. She now develops sudden redness, swelling, and tenderness of her previously existing skin lesions, with mild facial edema and low- grade fever. CT of the chest shows multiple pulmonary nodules surrounded by a ground-glass “halo”. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line antifungal drug for this patient?
e:
The presentation is characteristic of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in an
immunocompromised patient. Goodman & Gilman states that voriconazole has superior efficacy and survival compared with conventional amphotericin B and is approved for initial treatment of invasive aspergillosis.

A 47-year-old woman with ovarian carcinoma is receiving combination chemotherapy. After several treatment cycles, she develops progressive fatigue, reduced urine output, and a rise in serum creatinine. Laboratory investigations also show hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia, suggesting renal tubular electrolyte wasting. Her renal function had been normal before chemotherapy was started. Which of the following anticancer
drugs is most likely responsible for this adverse effect?
e: Nephrotoxicity is a major adverse effect of cisplatin. Cisplatin-induced tubular damage can produce renal electrolyte wasting, particularly hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, and hypophosphatemia. Pretreatment hydration and chloride diuresis can reduce its renal toxicity.

A 46-year-old woman is scheduled to receive high-dose cyclophosphamide as part of chemotherapy for a malignant disorder. The oncologist explains that one of its
metabolites, acrolein, can accumulate in the urinary tract and produce hemorrhagic cystitis, presenting with dysuria and hematuria.The physician decides to administer a protective drug along with chemotherapy to prevent this complication. Which of the following drugs should be given?
e: Cyclophosphamide produces the urotoxic metabolite acrolein, which can cause severe hemorrhagic cystitis. Mesna (2-mercaptoethanesulfonate) conjugates acrolein in the urine and prevents this toxicity.
